checker: Claude (Opus 5.5), independent adversarial checker, round 7; did not write or edit these reels. Every quote was machine-matched against its pinned source (all exact). Both whole reels were read in reels.json, and every frame's narration hash was recomputed with src/explore/narrationText.ts (all current).

units.evidence: [Wikipedia: Santos-Dumont 14-bis] "was a pioneer era, canard-style biplane designed and built by Brazilian aviation pioneer Alberto Santos-Dumont" (exact).
units.note: The only cut is 'that' ('a biplane that Alberto...' became 'a biplane Alberto...'). The meaning is unchanged, and 'designed and built' is the source's own wording. The caveat from round 4 still applies and still leaves the claim true: the same article says he 'commissioned [Voisin] to help him construct' it. The spoken line is the caption word for word, with '14-bis' respelled 'fourteen-bees' and 'Santos-Dumont' respelled 'Santos-Doomon'. In the reel, m3 does show the 14-bis (in its 12 November form), and frame 3 dates the photo.

units.evidence: [Wikipedia: Alberto Santos-Dumont] "on 23 October 1906 flew about 60 metres at a height of two to three metres ... at the Bagatelle Gamefield in Paris, taking off unassisted by an external launch system." and, in the 'On 23 October ... Oiseau de Proie II' paragraph, "The plane lifted off and flew for 60 metres, without taking advantage of headwinds, ramps, catapults, slopes, or other devices." (both exact).
units.note: Two cuts: 'off the ground' became 'up', and 'to launch it' was dropped. Neither loses anything. 'A few metres up' still covers the 2 to 3 m here and the 3 to 5 m in the 14-bis article. A catapult or ramp is a launch aid by definition, so 'with no catapult or ramp' still says the take-off was unassisted, and it is a true subset of the source's list. The date, the place (Bagatelle is in Paris) and 'about 60 metres' are unchanged. The frame is still the prediction reveal (reveal 1, answer 'About 60 metres'), and 'it' still refers back to the 14-bis named in frame 1. The spoken line matches the caption, with the date and number written out.

units.evidence: [Wikipedia: Alberto Santos-Dumont] "On 12 November in front of a crowd, he flew 220 metres at a height of six metres."; "he took off against the wind and flew 220 metres, for 21 seconds at an average speed of 37.4 km/h"; [Commons file page] "Nouveau triomphe de Santos-Dumont. 12 novembre 1906" (all exact).
units.note: Only the comma before 'in 21 seconds' was dropped and 'photograph' became 'photo'. Both quotes describe the same 4:45 pm flight of 220 m on 12 November, so joining the crowd, the distance and the time in one clause is accurate. The '22 seconds' in the 14-bis article was settled in earlier rounds: 220 m at 37.4 km/h is about 21.2 s, so '21 seconds' is the better-supported figure. 'This photo' is m3, the BnF/Jules Beau photo captioned 12 novembre 1906, which is the same picture shown in frames 1 and 2. The frame has no 'say', so the voice reads the caption as written.

units.evidence: [Wikipedia: Alberto Santos-Dumont] "Santos-Dumont is a national hero in Brazil, where it is popularly held that he preceded the Wright brothers in demonstrating a practical aeroplane." (exact). The 14-bis article adds that the 1903 Wright Flyer "accomplished takeoffs in a strong headwind without a catapult and made controlled and sustained flight; nearly three years before Santos-Dumont".
units.note: This round's cuts are harmless. 'Honours him as' became 'counts him', which still matches 'is a national hero', and 'that' was dropped. The problem is older wording that this check covers ('no qualifier dropped'): the quote's 'in demonstrating' is missing. The source reports a narrow Brazilian belief, that he was first to DEMONSTRATE a practical aeroplane, meaning publicly and without a launch aid. The caption turns it into a broad one, that he 'beat the Wright brothers to a practical aeroplane', which reads as being first to have one at all. That matters here because the next frame (f6) opens 'The first powered, controlled aeroplane to fly was the Wright brothers' Flyer'. Against the broad wording, f6 reads as a rebuttal of Brazil, which sets up a weaker version of the belief than the source records. The source's version does not conflict with f6. The caption is still a fair report that many Brazilians credit him, so this is imprecise, not wrong.
units.fix: Restore the qualifier with one short word: 'Brazil counts him a national hero, and many there hold he beat the Wright brothers to showing a practical aeroplane.' The frame has no 'say', so the voice reads the new caption. Re-narrate the reel: it runs 49.11 s now, and one extra word adds roughly 0.3 s, which keeps it under 50 s.
units.resolved: Now "…hold he beat the Wright brothers to showing a practical aeroplane." (re-narrated)

units.evidence: [Wikipedia: Survival of the fittest] "Darwin promptly replied ... I fully agree with all that you say on the advantages of H. Spencer's excellent expression of 'the survival of the fittest'. This however had not occurred to me till reading your letter." and "In On the Origin of Species, he introduced the phrase in the fifth edition published in 1869" (both exact).
units.note: Cuts: 'wrote back' became 'replied' (the source's own word), 'the advantages of Spencer's phrase' became 'the phrase's advantages', 'until he read the letter' became 'until that letter', and 'the fifth edition of the Origin' became 'the Origin's fifth edition'. The paraphrase still claims only that the ADVANTAGES had not occurred to Darwin, not the phrase itself. That is right, because he knew Spencer's 1864 usage. Dropping 'Spencer's' leaves no wrong reading in the reel: f1 and f2 set up 'the phrase' and 'his phrase' as Spencer's 'survival of the fittest', and f4 ends on 'Spencer's words'. The other phrase on screen in f4, 'natural selection', cannot be meant, since it was Darwin's own term. 'That letter' points back to Wallace's July 1866 letter (f3). 'He put it in the Origin's fifth edition, in 1869' does not claim this was his first use, which was Variation, 1868. The spoken line matches the caption, with the year written out. Minor clarity point, unchanged from earlier rounds and not a fact error: no frame before this one names On the Origin of Species, so some viewers will not know what 'the Origin' is.
